parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State what is meant by redshift.

markscheme_points.text: recession of galaxy (from observer) causes emitted light to have
increase in observed wavelength / decrease in observed frequency

hints: Hint 1: Think about what happens to the waves from a source that is moving away from you - do the wavefronts get stretched out or squashed together in your frame?
Hint 2: Link that stretching to light from a distant galaxy - which end of the visible spectrum has the longest wavelength, and what does this mean for the observed frequency?
parts.proper_answer: Light from a galaxy receding from the observer has an increase in observed wavelength (decrease in observed frequency) compared to the emitted wavelength.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture a galaxy moving away**
Imagine you are sitting still and a galaxy is rushing away from you while it emits light waves. Because it moves a little further away between emitting one wave crest and the next, the distance between crests as seen by you is stretched out.

Step 2: **Connect stretch to red**
A stretched light wave means a larger observed wavelength $\lambda_{obs} > \lambda_{emit}$ and therefore a lower observed frequency since $c = f\lambda$. Longer wavelengths are towards the red end of the spectrum, so the spectral lines are shifted towards red. That shift is what we call redshift, and it is evidence of recession.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Explain how observations of redshift lead to the idea that the universe is expanding.

markscheme_points.text: (distant) galaxies show redshift so galaxies are moving apart
galaxies moving apart means universe must be expanding

hints: Hint 1: Recall what you concluded in (a) about what redshift tells you about the motion of a single galaxy relative to Earth.
Hint 2: Now zoom out - if almost all distant galaxies in every direction show this same effect, what must be happening to the separations between galaxies over time?
parts.proper_answer: Distant galaxies show redshift, so they are receding and moving apart from each other. Increasing separation between galaxies means the universe is expanding.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **From redshift to moving apart**
Observations show that light from almost all distant galaxies is redshifted. From (a) you know redshift means recession from the observer. So galaxies are generally moving away from us and, importantly, away from each other.

Step 2: **From moving apart to expansion**
If the distances between galaxies are systematically increasing with time in all directions, space itself must be getting bigger. That is exactly what we mean by an expanding universe - it is not an explosion into existing space, but the increase of separations between galaxies.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Explain how Hubble's law leads to the Big Bang theory of the origin of the universe.

markscheme_points.text: the speed of recession is proportional to the distance of the galaxies from each other or more distant galaxies are receding faster

Any two points from: • more distant galaxies represent further back in time • a long time ago, all matter in the universe must have been very close together • a long time ago, all matter in the universe must have been moving apart very fast

hints: Hint 1: Start by recalling the pattern Hubble found between how far away a galaxy is and how fast it is moving away - which galaxies recede fastest?
Hint 2: Think backwards in time like running a film in reverse - if everything is moving apart now, where must everything have been a very long time ago?
Hint 3: Consider what light from very distant galaxies tells you about the past, and what it implies about how close together and how fast-moving matter must have been at the beginning.
parts.proper_answer: Hubble's law states recession speed $v$ is proportional to distance $d$, with more distant galaxies receding faster. Running time backwards, all matter must have been very close together and moving apart very fast a long time ago, consistent with a Big Bang origin. More distant galaxies are seen as they were further back in time.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **State Hubble's law clearly**
Hubble found that recession speed is proportional to distance: $$v = H_{0}d$$ where $H_{0}$ is the Hubble constant. In words, the more distant a galaxy is from us, the faster it is receding.

Step 2: **Run the expansion backwards**
If galaxies are moving apart now, with distant ones moving fastest, then going back in time they must have been closer together. Go back far enough and all the matter in the universe must have been concentrated in a very small, very dense and hot state.

Step 3: **Link to the Big Bang and look-back time**
That idea of the universe starting from an extremely compact state and then expanding rapidly apart is the Big Bang theory. It is strengthened because light takes time to travel, so more distant galaxies are observed as they were further back in time, showing the universe was denser in the past and that matter must have been moving apart very fast at the beginning.
